title: Tillage
description: Preparation of soil by mechanical agitation
wiki_lead:
Tillage is the agricultural preparation of soil by mechanical agitation of various types, such as digging, stirring, and overturning. Examples of human-powered tilling methods using hand tools include shoveling, picking, mattock work, hoeing, and raking. Examples of draft-animal-powered or mechanized work include ploughing (overturning with moldboards or chiseling with chisel shanks), rototilling, rolling with cultipackers or other rollers, harrowing, and cultivating with cultivator shanks (teeth).
Tillage that is deeper and more thorough is classified as primary, and tillage that is shallower and sometimes more selective of location is secondary. Primary tillage such as ploughing tends to produce a rough surface finish, whereas secondary tillage tends to produce a smoother surface finish, such as that required to make a good seedbed for many crops. Harrowing and rototilling often combine primary and secondary tillage into one operation.
"Tillage" can also mean the land that is tilled. The word "cultivation" has several senses that overlap substantially with those of "tillage". In a general context, both can refer to agriculture. Within agriculture, both can refer to any kind of soil agitation. Additionally, "cultivation" or "cultivating" may refer to an even narrower sense of shallow, selective secondary tillage of row crop fields that kills weeds while sparing the crop plants.

Definitions
Primary tillage loosens the soil and mixes in fertilizer or plant material, resulting in soil with a rough texture.
Secondary tillage produces finer soil and sometimes shapes the rows, preparing the seed bed. It also provides weed control throughout the growing season during the maturation of the crop plants, unless such weed control is instead achieved with low-till or no-till methods involving herbicides.

The seedbed preparation can be done with harrows (of which there are many types and subtypes), dibbles, hoes, shovels, rotary tillers, subsoilers, ridge- or bed-forming tillers, rollers, or cultivators.
The weed control, to the extent that it is done via tillage, is usually achieved with cultivators or hoes, which disturb the top few centimeters of soil around the crop plants but with minimal disturbance of the crop plants themselves. The tillage kills the weeds via two mechanisms: uprooting them, burying their leaves (cutting off their photosynthesis), or a combination of both. Weed control both prevents the crop plants from being outcompeted by the weeds (for water and sunlight) and prevents the weeds from reaching their seed stage, thus reducing future weed population aggressiveness.


History

Tilling was first performed via human labor, sometimes involving slaves. Hoofed animals could also be used to till soil by trampling, in addition to pigs, whose natural instincts are to root the ground regularly if allowed to. The wooden plow was then invented. (It is difficult to pinpoint the exact date of its invention. However, the earliest evidence of plow usage dates back to around 4000 BCE in Mesopotamia (modern-day Iraq) . It could be pulled with human labor, or by mule, ox, elephant, water buffalo, or a similar sturdy animal. Horses are generally unsuitable, though breeds such as the Clydesdale were bred as draft animals.
Tilling could at times be very labor-intensive. This aspect is discussed in the 16th-century French agronomic text written by Charles Estienne:

A raw, rough, and tough soil is hard to till and will neither bring forth corn, nor any other thing without great labor, however the seasons be temperate in moisture and dryness ... you must labor it most exquisitely, harrow it and manure it very oft with great store of dung, so you shall make it better ... but especially desire that they may not be watered with rain, for water is as good as poison to them.

grok_lead: Tillage is the mechanical manipulation of the soil in agricultural practices, primarily aimed at preparing seedbeds, managing crop residues, incorporating amendments such as fertilizers, controlling weeds and pests, and alleviating surface compaction and rutting. This process has been integral to crop production for millennia, facilitating aeration to promote seed germination, root growth, and overall soil permeability for moisture and air. By turning or loosening the soil, tillage traditionally disrupts weed cycles and buries plant debris, though modern approaches balance these benefits against environmental impacts. The history of tillage traces back to ancient civilizations, where early farmers, including Native Americans before European settlement, employed simple handheld digging sticks to disturb soil for planting. With the arrival of European settlers, practices evolved to include horse- and oxen-drawn wooden implements, which gradually transitioned to more durable iron and steel tools by the 19th century. The advent of mechanized agriculture in the early 20th century, fueled by the rise of tractors and internal combustion engines, enabled deeper and more intensive soil inversion through plows and harrows, revolutionizing large-scale farming but also accelerating soil degradation. The Dust Bowl catastrophe of the 1930s in the United States, resulting from excessive plowing of native grasslands, exposed the vulnerabilities of conventional tillage to erosion and drought, spurring federal soil conservation efforts and the development of reduced-tillage strategies. Contemporary tillage systems are broadly categorized into conventional and conservation types, each with distinct implements and objectives. Conventional tillage relies on multiple field passes using primary tools like moldboard plows for deep soil inversion (typically 6-12 inches) and secondary implements such as disk harrows or field cultivators to create a fine, uniform seedbed while fully incorporating residues. This approach effectively controls weeds and pests but can degrade soil structure over time by fracturing aggregates and exposing organic matter to rapid decomposition. In response, conservation tillage emerged as a sustainable alternative, defined as any method that disturbs less than 30% of the soil surface and retains at least 30% crop residue cover post-planting to mitigate erosion. Key variants include no-till, which avoids soil disturbance entirely by planting directly into residue-covered fields; strip-till, which prepares narrow bands for seeds; ridge-till, involving raised ridges for planting; and mulch-till, which lightly mixes residues into the topsoil. These systems, often employing specialized tools like chisel plows with sweeps or vertical tillage disks, promote soil health by enhancing organic matter accumulation, improving water infiltration, and fostering microbial activity. The importance of tillage in modern agriculture lies in its role in optimizing crop yields while addressing environmental challenges, though excessive use has historically contributed to soil erosion, loss of biodiversity, and increased greenhouse gas emissions from organic matter oxidation. Conservation practices counteract these issues by conserving soil moisture more effectively than conventional methods, reducing fuel and labor inputs by minimizing passes, and limiting nutrient runoff into waterways. In the United States, adoption of no-till and reduced-tillage systems has grown significantly since the 1990s, covering about 72% of cropland as of 2017, with rates continuing to increaseâfor example, reaching 69% for wheat in 2022âdriven by economic incentives and policy support for sustainable farming. Ongoing research emphasizes integrating tillage with cover crops and precision technologies, such as GPS-guided implements, to further enhance soil resilience in the face of climate variability.
